subject: modeling observation as a function of two random quantities

messages.author: f17ec5a3936c7373
messages.subject: modeling observation as a function of two random quantities
parts:
I asked this on StackOverflow a few months ago and the response was RTFM and then the question was deleted.  I haven't been able to find an answer in the manual (I have stan-reference-2.9.0).  If the answer is in the manual (which I bet it is), a pointer to the appropriate section or model example would be a wonderful answer to this question.

How can I model my observations as the sum of two random variables?  As a simplest possible example, imagine I observe a quantity that I know to be the sum of one draw from normal distribution A (with unknown parameters) and one draw from gamma distribution B (with unknown parameters).  Of course I have prior information on the parameters of A and B.

I've set it up like this:


data {
  int<lower=1> N;   // number of observations
}

parameters {
    real mu_a;
    real mu_b;
    real<lower = 0> sigma;
    real a;
    real b;
}

model {
    mu_a ~ normal(0, 10);
    sigma_a ~ gamma(1, 1);
    a ~ normal(mu_a, sigma_a);

    alpha_b ~ normal(2, 5);
    beta_b ~ normal(2, 5);
    b ~ gamma(alpha_b, beta_b);
}

generated quantities {
    vector[N] w;      // observed quantity
    w <- a + b;
}



And the error I get is:

PARSER EXPECTED: <expression assignable to left-hand side>
which points to the line with "w <- a + b;"

Originally, I declared w in the data block (which makes sense to me), but StackOverflow user http://stats.stackexchange.com/users/35989/tim stated with great confidence that it should be in the generated quantities block, so I moved it.

parts:

> data {

> }

> real mu_a;
> real mu_b;
> real<lower = 0> sigma;
> real a;
> real b;
> }
>
> model {
> mu_a ~ normal(0, 10);
> sigma_a ~ gamma(1, 1);
> a ~ normal(mu_a, sigma_a);
>
> alpha_b ~ normal(2, 5);
> beta_b ~ normal(2, 5);
> b ~ gamma(alpha_b, beta_b);
> }
>
> generated quantities {
> vector[N] w; // observed quantity
> w <- a + b;
> }

> And the error I get is:
>
> PARSER EXPECTED: <expression assignable to left-hand side>

> which points to the line with "w <- a + b;”

Something is suppressing most of the parser error message. That’s
just the last bit.

The immediate problem is that you’re trying to assign a scalar (a + b)
to a vector (w), which is not possible. You have to broadcast the
scalar values to each component of the vector, for example by

w <- rep_vector(a + b, N);

The next problem is that a measurement model needs to go in the model
block, not generated quantities. I have no idea what model you
really want to build, but I imagine it would be something like

model {
mu_a ~ normal(0, 10);
sigma_a ~ gamma(1, 1);
a ~ normal(mu_a, sigma_a);

alpha_b ~ normal(2, 5);
beta_b ~ normal(2, 5);
b ~ gamma(alpha_b, beta_b);

w ~ normal(a + b, sigma);
}

Then there’s the problem that alpha_b and beta_b and sigma_a and
sigma_b need to be defined somewhere. Also b needs to be declared
as positive or you’ll run into problems.

Long story short, your model needs lots of work. I recommend playing
with some of the simpler examples in the manual first.

Michael,

Thanks for your response.  It seems that in my attempt to make a toy example of my problem, I introduced a load of simple errors that obscured the problem.  I can deal with all those errors, and I've included below my draft of the model I really want to build, along with an R program to simulate data for it, which I think is clean from those types of errors.

The key piece of the discussion is your recommendation to add this line to the model block:
w ~ normal(a + b, sigma);

But I think that conveys a pretty different idea than what I'm going for.  I don't believe that my observation is the sum of a, b, and noise.  I actually believe that my observation is an essentially noiseless function of a and b.  Like a mathematical function where the input precisely specifies the output.  I believe my observation is the sum of a and b.  Maybe I should use the modeling approach you suggest and place a strong prior on sigma that keeps it very close to zero?  It seems that any non-zero-ness of sigma, however, would hurt my estimates of the parameters of the distributions from which a and b come.









The idea here is that I arrive at some time during a process (my co-worker taking a shower in a shared locker room), and I want to infer the mean and standard deviation of his shower durations.  I assume that I arrive at a time uniformly distributed between the start and end of the shower.

library(rstan)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

library(truncnorm)

N <- 100
mu <- 35
sigma <- 5

durations <- rtruncnorm(n = N, mean = mu, sd = sigma, a = 0)
arrivals <- runif(n = N, min = 0, max = durations)
waits <- durations - arrivals

fit1 <- stan(file = 'z_shower_waiting.stan',
             data = list(N = N, w = waits))

data {
  int<lower=1> N;   // number of observations

vector[N] w;      // observed wait time
}


parameters {
  real<lower = 0> mu;
  real<lower = 0> sigma;
  vector<lower = 0.1>[N] d; // duration of shower
  vector[N] a;              // arrival time of waiter (me)
}


model {
  d ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  a ~ uniform(0, d);
  w <- d - a;
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] modeling observation as a function of two random quantities
parts:
The standard thing to do would be to model when he starts
the shower and how long the shower lasts.

Can you assume exactly one shower/day?

Anything you know about when it is and how long it is
a priori?

What exactly do you observe? Arrival time and if or if
not a shower going on? Do you have shower end time if
you arrive during the shower? Shower start and end time
if you arrive before the shower?

If you always arrive during a shower and don't observe
when showers end, you won't be able to estimate duration
because the model won't be identifiable. Otherwise, you
have censoring of a start or end time --- see the chapter
on censored data in the model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] modeling observation as a function of two random quantities
parts:
Bob,

Thanks for your continued thought on this question.

On Saturday, December 26, 2015 at 9:15:52 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The standard thing to do would be to model when he starts
the shower and how long the shower lasts.

That could get hairy because we both arrive at work at highly erratic times -- some days I arrive early for an early meeting, other days I sleep in, other days I arrive in the afternoon, etc.  I can't say anything about the distribution of my arrival time or the distribution of his arrival time.
Can you assume exactly one shower/day?

Maybe one shower per day, but certainly not one observation per day.  If I arrive at the locker room before this guy, I take my shower and go on with my day and don't observe anything about his shower duration.  If I arrive after his shower is done, I don't observe anything about his shower duration.  So I would say a maximum of one observation per day.  Most days no observation at all.

Anything you know about when it is and how long it is
a priori?

I summarize my prior information (based on knowledge of how long it takes most humans to shower) in the following way.

prior on mean shower duration is truncated normal, centered on 15, with sd = 5, left-truncation at 0 and no right-truncation.

prior on precision of shower duration is gamma(0.2, 0.1).  I would be happy with any not-too-informative prior here.  I know half-t has been recommended in some cases.
What exactly do you observe?
Only how long I wait.

Arrival time and if or if
not a shower going on?
No.

Do you have shower end time if
you arrive during the shower?
No, but I know how long I waited.  If I make a new clock and start it when I arrive, then on that clock's time, I have the shower end time.

Shower start and end time
if you arrive before the shower?
No observation if I arrive before he starts the shower.

If you always arrive during a shower and don't observe
when showers end, you won't be able to estimate duration
because the model won't be identifiable.

How can you tell that it's non-identifiable?  Oftentimes, when I believe a model is non-identifiable, I try to think of two parameter sets that have the same probability distribution.  But I haven't been able to think of any for this problem yet.

Otherwise, you
have censoring of a start or end time --- see the chapter
on censored data in the model.

- Bob

I'd start by giving you both start times and
durations and using your observations as censored.
Normal would be easy to start, but you could go to
some kind of non-parametric model like a GP in the end.

All times are wall clock times.

If you arrive while he's showering, you don't know
when the shower starts, but you know when it ends.

If he arrives while you're showering, same information,
but reversed.

If you shower without seeing him, you only know his
shower started and ended before you got there or started
and ended after you get there.

Then just set up the model.

- Bob

> > > The immediate problem is that you’re trying to assign a scalar (a + b)
> > > to a vector (w), which is not possible. You have to broadcast the
> > > scalar values to each component of the vector, for example by
> > >
> > > w <- rep_vector(a + b, N);
> > >
> > > The next problem is that a measurement model needs to go in the model
> > > block, not generated quantities. I have no idea what model you
> > > really want to build, but I imagine it would be something like
> > >
> > > model {
> > > mu_a ~ normal(0, 10);
> > > sigma_a ~ gamma(1, 1);
> > > a ~ normal(mu_a, sigma_a);
> > >
> > > alpha_b ~ normal(2, 5);
> > > beta_b ~ normal(2, 5);
> > > b ~ gamma(alpha_b, beta_b);
> > >
> > > w ~ normal(a + b, sigma);
> > > }
> > >
> > > Then there’s the problem that alpha_b and beta_b and sigma_a and
> > > sigma_b need to be defined somewhere. Also b needs to be declared
> > > as positive or you’ll run into problems.
> > >
> > > Long story short, your model needs lots of work. I recommend playing
> > > with some of the simpler examples in the manual first.
